title: The Night 2 American Submarines Ambushed Japan's Entire Flagship Fleet
fullText: It is 1:00 in the morning on October 23rd, 1944. 32 Japanese warships are moving north through the darkness of the South China Sea. Five battleships, 10 heavy cruisers, 15 destroyers, moving in columns at 16 knots, their bow waves throwing pale cold fire. Bioluminescence churned up from the tropical deep against holes of gray steel. At the head of the port column, a heavy cruiser named a targetgo carries the flag of Vice Admiral Teo Kurita, the man commanding what is left of the Imperial Japanese Navy's surface strength. Behind a targetgo, steaming safely in line, are Yamato and Mousashi. Two of the largest warships ever built by any nation, each displacing more than 60,000 tons. Their 16-in gun turrets rising against the night sky like small fortress towers. This fleet is the last one. The Japanese Navy will not be able to assemble another like it. Somewhere in that formation, a radio operator aboard Yamato has just transcribed an intercepted American signal. It reads that American submarines are tracking the fleet. The report reaches Admiral Karita. He reads it. He does not change course. He does not order screening destroyers forward to sweep ahead of his cruiser columns. He does nothing with the information at all. What was he thinking? Overconfidence? Fatalism. The cold arithmetic of a man who has fought for three years and understands that somewhere in every ocean there are always submarines and that worrying about them is like worrying about the sea itself. We cannot know. His postwar interrogations were sparse. He left no diary. We have only what he did and what he did not do. 150 mi to the south, a radar screen aboard a submerged American submarine shows a contact at the southern entrance to Palawan Passage. The operator stares at it. It looks at first like a rain squall. Then it resolves. It is not a rain squall. He calls the captain. By October 1944, the Imperial Japanese Navy has been systematically broken. At Midway, it lost four fleet carriers and the cream of its naval aviation. At the Philippine Sea, the following June, it lost three more and any realistic chance of rebuilding. What remains are the surface ships, the cruisers, the destroyers, the two super battleships. And these are being masked for one final operation designed not to win the war, but to prevent its immediate loss. The operation is called Showgo One. Its target is the American invasion fleet at Lady Gulf in the central Philippines. The Philippines are not a strategic afterthought. They are the spine of Japan's entire supply chain. Every tanker from the Dutch East Indies oil fields that keeps Japan's war economy running has to pass through Philippine waters. If the Philippines fall, that chain is cut. The home islands starve. The warships that survive, sitting on empty fuel tanks in Japanese ports, become monuments. Kurita's center force is the killing blow. Five battleships, 10 heavy cruisers, two light cruisers, 15 destroyers based near Singapore because American submarines have already reduced the Japanese home islands fuel reserves to a trickle. And the fleet must stay close to its supply. This is not a fleet sent to fight on equal terms. This is an Empire's last throw of the dice and it is sailing straight into Palawan passage. Two American submarines are waiting. Though at this hour neither crew yet knows exactly what they are waiting for. USS Darter is a Gateau class fleet submarine 311 ft long built in Groutton, Connecticut. Commissioned in September 1943. She carries 24 torpedoes in 10 tubes, six forward, four out, and a mechanical brain called the target data computer that processes bearing rates, ranges, and speeds into firing solutions. Her captain is Commander David Haywood Mcclintok, 32 years old. He spent the earliest and most dangerous years of Pacific submarine warfare attacking Japanese warships with torpedoes that regularly refused to detonate and the admirals who wouldn't hear complaints about them. He earned a silver star attacking a Japanese cruiser at close range in a night surface engagement. His crew by every account loved him. He had a dry wit and steady nerves and they had learned the difference between the two. USS Dace is his partner. Same class, same armament commanded by Commander Bladen Claget. And together the two boats form a Wolfpack with Mcccleinto holding tactical control. They are patrolling Palawan Passage, a deep water channel 35 to 40 mi wide running between the island of Paloan to the east and the South China Sea to the west. The western edge of that channel is marked on every reliable nautical chart with a phrase that appears more than once and is never meant as poetry. The charts call it dangerous ground. It is an expanse of uncharted coral reefs and shaw water running for hundreds of miles without reliable soundings without adequate surveys. A maze of reef and reef shadow that has been claiming ships since before the age of steam. It is the only navigational hazard in this stretch of ocean the Japanese haven't put on anyone's chart with any precision. The name will matter before this story is over. At 116 on October 23rd, the blip on Dart's radar resolves. The operator's first instinct is a rain squall. A common return in tropical waters familiar enough that a good operator knows what it looks like. This doesn't look like that. The return is too solid, too structured, and it is moving north at a speed that rains squalls do not move. Mcccleintok is called to the Conning Tower. Within minutes, the picture is unmistakable. Dozens of contacts, a formation the size of a small city stretching across the southern mouth of Palawan Passage. The Japanese fleet, which American naval intelligence had completely lost track of for several days, has just announced itself on a radar screen aboard a 311 ft submarine. Dart immediately transmits her contact report to Allied command. The flash reaches headquarters within the hour and triggers responses across the entire Pacific theater. Naval historian Samuel Elliot Morrison will later call those transmissions the most significant reports of the Pacific War. The irony is that Mcccleintoch's report has the fleet's composition wrong. He doesn't yet know precisely what he is looking at. It doesn't matter. The intelligence is imprecise in its particulars and correct in every way that counts. But acting takes time. And Dart and Dace are already moving. For 5 hours, both submarines run at full surface speed, chasing the formation from behind, cutting a diagonal course to get ahead of it. 5 hours of engines at maximum revolutions, spray over the bridge, the eastern sky, beginning its slow conversion from black to purple to gray. They have to be ahead of the fleet before first light. Once submerged, they can make barely eight knots. The Japanese are making 16. The window is closing with every mile. What Darter's radio room is broadcasting during those 5 hours, position updates, course corrections, speed estimates, is being intercepted aboard Yamato. The contact report reaches Karita for the second time. This time it is not an ambiguous intercept. This is an American submarine transmitting in real time, which means an American submarine is very close. The screening destroyers remain in their columns. The fleet does not slow. The course does not change. At 4:30, Dart is ahead of the Japanese port column. Dace is positioned against the starboard. Both submarines dive. The crews go to battle stations. The TDC operators begin asking for range. In the growing light of nautical dawn, enormous silhouettes are beginning to separate from the horizon. Capital ships moving in formation at 60 knots, completely unaware. At 524, Mcccleintoch fires. Six torpedoes leave Dart's forward tubes at near point blank range aimed at the lead ship of the port column. That ship is a targetgo, the flagship of Japan's center force. She is 668 ft long, 10 8 in guns, 889 men. Too kurita on her flag bridge. Four torpedoes find her. Aboard a targetgo. A sailor named Matsu Yoshitsucha is resting near the ship's shrine on the middle deck. He is 24 years old. He will live to be 101 and when interviewers find him in 2022, one of the last surviving combatants of the entire battle of Lady Gulf. His account is brief. No one could say a word. he says. Young soldiers running around, jumping into the sea. The order to abandon ship comes within minutes. Karita descends the gangway ladder. Men go over the side. 600 m a stern aboard the heavy cruiser Takao. A sailor named Nakagawa watches from his deck. In the pitch blackness, he will recall, a big red flame rose up, and I could clearly see that the Atago had been hit. He watches the flame and does not yet know that two more torpedoes from Dart's stern tubes are already in the water, heading for him. Inside Dart's hull, 8 minutes after the hits on a targetgo, the crew hears the ship breaking apart through the pressure hull itself. A grinding, cracking report transmitted through seawater and steel. A targetgo capsizes at 553, 18 minutes after she was hit. She takes 360 men to the bottom with her, including her captain. Karita is in the water. The Japanese formation does what doctrine demands. It turns away from the attack, wheeling to starboard to present the smallest possible silhouette to the threat on its port side. Standard anti-ubmarine maneuvering. Every officer in the fleet is following exactly the correct procedure. The trouble is that turning away from Dart turns directly toward Dace. Claget has been watching. The starboard column is swinging toward him, closing the range, feeding itself into his firing solution. At 556, Dace fires six torpedoes at the lead ship of the approaching column. Claget believes he is shooting at a Congo class battleship. He is not. The target is the heavy cruiser Mayer. Same class as a targetgo. Approximately a thousand men aboard. Four torpedoes hit. Mia rolls over and goes down in 7 minutes. 336 men die. Claget sweeps his periscope across the scene. Japanese destroyers are firing in every direction. The water around a targetgo. Maya is going. He calls out to everyone in the conning tower. It looks like the 4th of July out there. One is sinking and the other is burning. The Japs are firing all over the place. What a show. Then he turns the periscope toward the next target. Stand by for a setup, he says. The Japanese destroyers drop depth charges. Both submarines go deep and absorb the attack. Neither take significant damage. The Japanese are firing at guesses. The clock reads 556. 32 minutes have passed since Mcccleintok fired. Two Japanese heavy cruisers are on the bottom of Palawan Passage. A third Takao struck by Darter's stern torpedoes. Three boiler rooms flooded. Two propeller shafts shattered is dead in the water. Two destroyers have been stripped from the strike force to escort her back to Brunai. 696 men are dead. The most powerful naval force Japan can put to sea has had its center column destroyed before it has even cleared the South China Sea. And the man commanding that force is swimming for his life. Karita is hauled aboard the destroyer Kishinami. His fleet steams on without him. It takes 9 hours before he can transfer from Kishinami to Yamato and reassume command. 9 hours during which the fleet presses north on standing orders. The staff scattered, the flagship gone, command fallen to Vice Admiral Ugaki on Yamato. The fleet does not stop. It cannot. But it has no Kurita for 9 hours. Later, years later, Rear Admiral Tumiji Coyanagi, who was Karita's chief of staff and who swam out of Palawan Passage alongside him, writes about what happened in a candid essay published in the United States Naval Institute proceedings in 1953. He puts into words what the Japanese naval staff had always known and never acted on. They had always believed, he writes, that a Yamato class battleship should have been the flagship for this operation. But combined fleet rejected the idea. Doctrine held that the commanding officer must ride a cruiser, the key ship of night surface engagements. Combined fleet had never abandoned this traditional principle, and the sinking of a targetgo proved them wrong. Karita was not on a targetgo because of bad luck. He was on a targetgo because his own navy's doctrine demanded it. The same Yamato that had been steaming safely behind him, 60,000 tons of armored steel, effectively unsinkable, was the ship he should have been standing on. Japan's fleet doctrine had not been revised in 3 years of war that had rendered it obsolete at every point. Two American submarines didn't just exploit a gap in Karita's anti-ubmarine screen. They exploited a gap in the institutional logic of the Imperial Japanese Navy itself. The man who arrives on Yamato's bridge 9 hours later, exhausted, carrying the physical memory of the South China Sea, is the same man who will make the most debated tactical decision of the entire Pacific War in 2 days time. Dart and Dace don't leave. Taka is still out there making for Brunai, under escort, slow and wounded. Both submarine commanders agree she has to be finished. In the afternoon of October 23rd, Dart makes a submerged approach and is driven off by the screening destroyers before she can fire. Mcccleintoch notes the failure. He plans for that night. There is a problem he has not been able to account for. Data hasn't surfaced since before the attack. Her navigational plot, the running calculation of position that every submarine depends on, is now more than 24 hours old. She is dead reckoning through the most reef studded waters in the South China Sea without being able to verify where she actually is. She is navigating on math and memory in hostile waters in darkness. At 2200 on October 23rd, Taka gets underway again. Mcccleintoch plans an endound a fast surface run to get ahead of the cruiser and attack from her bow. He allows a margin of seven miles around Bombay Shaw, a coral reef on the western side of the passage. He estimates the current at approximately 1 knot. He's wrong by a quarter of a knot. At 00005 on October the 24th, USS Darta moving at 17 knots through the tropical darkness rides up onto Bombay Shaw. The forward draft goes to 9 ft. She is on coral in the middle of dangerous ground. She cannot move and she is 300 m from any friendly port. Dace responds immediately. She lies to 50 yards off Dart's beam while Dart's crew attempts to back off the reef. dumps fuel to lighten the bow, waits for the tide. Nothing works. A Japanese destroyer closes to 12,000 yards, appears to ready its guns, and then inexplicably turns away and rejoins Takao. At 2:45, Dace passes a messenger line across 50 yards of open water. Sailors crossed between the submarines in rubber boats in the darkness, carrying nothing but themselves, leaving behind three war patrols of accumulated belongings. Mcclinuk is the last man off. He watches the demolition charges fire at 455. They fail. The hull holds. Dace fires her remaining torpedoes at Dart. They strike the reef and explode short. She pumps 214-in shells into the wreck. A Japanese aircraft forces both submarines under before more can be done. In the days that follow, USS Rock is called in and fires 10 torpedoes. Same result. USS Nautilus arrives and delivers 556-in shells into the carcass. By Nautilus's own assessment, the draft is down to 4 ft. She is firing at the reef. Data does not sink. Before any of that begins, a Japanese boarding party reaches the wreck. The crew has destroyed the electronics, the codes, the navigation equipment, but the hull is intact. Part of the classified technical library survives. Japanese naval intelligence recovers it. The submarine that fired the most consequential torpedoes of the battle of Laty Gulf has also handed the enemy an intelligence windfall. Mcccleintoch is not held responsible. The finding is that what happened on Bombay show was the compounding of small errors under conditions of extreme operational pressure and that the grounding was one of those unfortunate losses that war exacts. His crew is saved. Every last man he brings one thing off Dart. Not his wife's photograph, not his watch. Her favorite ashtray. My wife always said I'd have been more popular. He noted in an interview years later, "If I'd rescued her picture instead of that ashtray." Karita presses on. On October 24th, his battered center force enters the Cibuan Sea. American carrier aircraft attack in waves. The super battleship Mousashi, 60,000 tons. The largest ship in the world absorbs 19 torpedo hits and 17 bombs before she rolls over and goes down. The rest of the force passes through San Bernardino Strait during the night of October 24th and emerges into the Philippine Sea. On the morning of October 25th, Karita's ships fall on the American escort carriers and destroyers off the island of Samar. A handful of thin-kinned ships completely outgunned. Destroyers and destroyer escorts and slow carriers built on merchant hulls. They should be destroyed in an hour. Kurita breaks off the action and withdraws. He turns the center force around and leads it back through San Bernardino Straight. Historians have argued about that decision ever since. Some reconstructed from tactical confusion, misidentified targets, failed communications, the conviction that American submarines and aircraft were converging from every direction. Others note the degradation of the force, the collapse of the coordinated plan, the two days of unrelenting air attack that preceded those final hours. All of these things are true. None of them, individually or together, fully explains the withdrawal. What the record allows us to say is this. Kurita arrived at Samar physically depleted, carrying the weight of two days that had included being thrown into the South China Sea, 9 hours of recovery aboard a destroyer, and watching Mousashi go down from Yamato's bridge. He arrived at the moment of decision already diminished. How much of what happened off Samar on October 25th was decided in the water of Palawan passage on October 23rd? We cannot say with certainty. We only know the two events are connected in ways that history cannot fully untangle. Kurita survived the war. He gave sparse answers to American interrogators after the surrender. He died in 1977. He never fully explained the withdrawal and he was never pressed into one. The Atarago lies in 1,800 m of water in Palawan Passage. Maya is close by. Takao was towed to Singapore, declared unreparable, surrendered to the British in September 1945, sunk as a target ship in 1946. The only ship of her class to outlast the war, and she never fired another shot in it. Claget brought Dart's crew safely to Australia. Both boats received the Navy unit commendation. Mcccleintoch was awarded the Navy Cross in February 1945 and persuaded Admiral King himself to authorize the transfer of his entire Dart crew together to a new submarine USS Menhaden so they could go on fighting together. He lived to 89. He died in 2002 in Marquette, Michigan. USS Darta sat on Bombay Shaw for decades. A Navy salvage party arrived in 1951 and detonated the torpedoes remaining in her forward room, blowing off the bow. By 1998, her deteriorated remains could still be seen at low tide. A rusting outline lying on the coral. As of 2023, there is no visible evidence of the wreck above the surface. She has subsided completely into the reef. The submarine that spotted Japan's last fleet, that transmitted the most important contact reports of the Pacific War, that sank the flagship of the center force in 18 minutes and crippled a second cruiser before the minute hand had moved, has simply disappeared into the place where the nautical charts printed their oldest warning. It turned out to be dangerous for everyone.
fullTextVi: Bây giờ là 1h sáng ngày 23/10/1944. 32 tàu chiến Nhật Bản đang di chuyển về phía bắc xuyên qua bóng tối của Biển Đông. Năm thiết giáp hạm, 10 tàu tuần dương hạng nặng, 15 tàu khu trục, di chuyển theo hàng dọc với tốc độ 16 hải lý/giờ, của chúng sóng cung ném lửa lạnh nhạt. Sự phát quang sinh học bùng lên từ vùng sâu nhiệt đới trên những lỗ thép xám. Ở đầu cột cảng, một tàu tuần dương hạng nặng mang tên targetgo chở lá cờ của Phó đô đốc Teo Kurita, người chỉ huy những gì còn lại của sức mạnh bề mặt của Hải quân Đế quốc Nhật Bản. Phía sau mục tiêu đang di chuyển an toàn theo hàng là Yamato và Mousashi. Hai trong số những tàu chiến lớn nhất từng được một quốc gia chế tạo, mỗi chiếc có lượng giãn nước lớn hơn 60.000 tấn. Những tháp súng 16 inch của họ nhô lên trên bầu trời đêm giống như những tháp pháo đài nhỏ. Hạm đội này là chiếc cuối cùng. Hải quân Nhật Bản sẽ không thể lắp ráp một chiếc tương tự như vậy. Ở đâu đó trong đội hình đó, nhân viên điều hành vô tuyến trên tàu Yamato vừa ghi lại một bị chặn tín hiệu của Mỹ. Nó viết rằng các tàu ngầm Mỹ đang theo dõi hạm đội. Báo cáo đến tai Đô đốc Karita. Anh ấy đọc nó. Anh ấy không thay đổi hướng đi. Ông ta không ra lệnh cho các tàu khu trục hộ tống tiến về phía trước để càn quét các đoàn tàu tuần dương của mình. Anh ta không làm gì với thông tin cả. Anh ấy đang nghĩ gì vậy? Quá tự tin? Chủ nghĩa chí mạng. Số học lạnh lùng của một người đã chiến đấu suốt ba năm và hiểu được rằng ở đâu đó trên mỗi đại dương luôn có tàu ngầm và điều đó khiến chúng lo lắng giống như lo lắng về biển vậy. Chúng tôi không thể biết. Các cuộc thẩm vấn sau chiến tranh của ông rất thưa thớt. Anh ấy không để lại nhật ký. Chúng ta chỉ có những gì anh ấy đã làm và những gì anh ấy không làm. Cách đó 250 dặm về phía nam, màn hình radar trên tàu ngầm Mỹ hiển thị một địa chỉ liên lạc ở lối vào phía nam của Đoạn đường Palawan. Người điều hành nhìn chằm chằm vào nó. Thoạt nhìn nó giống như một cơn mưa rào. Sau đó nó giải quyết. Đó không phải là một cơn mưa rào. Anh gọi thuyền trưởng. Đến tháng 10 năm 1944, Hải quân Đế quốc Nhật Bản đã bị tan vỡ một cách có hệ thống. Tại Midway, họ mất bốn tàu sân bay và lực lượng không quân hải quân hùng mạnh. Tại biển Philippine, vào tháng 6 năm sau, nó mất thêm ba chiếc nữa và tất cả đều là thực tế cơ hội xây dựng lại. Những gì còn lại là các tàu mặt nước, tàu tuần dương, tàu khu trục, hai siêu thiết giáp hạm. Và những thứ này đang được che giấu cho một hoạt động cuối cùng được thiết kế để không giành được chiến tranh, nhưng để ngăn chặn sự mất mát ngay lập tức. Hoạt động này được gọi là Showgo One. Mục tiêu của nó là hạm đội xâm lược của Mỹ tại Lady Gulf ở miền trung Philippines. Philippines không phải là một lựa chọn chiến lược. Họ là xương sống của toàn bộ chuỗi cung ứng của Nhật Bản. Mọi tàu chở dầu từ các mỏ dầu Đông Ấn Hà Lan giữ vững nền kinh tế chiến tranh của Nhật Bản chạy phải đi qua vùng biển Philippines. Nếu Philippines sụp đổ, chuỗi đó sẽ bị cắt đứt. Các hòn đảo quê hương chết đói. Những tàu chiến sống sót, ngồi trên những thùng nhiên liệu rỗng ở cảng Nhật Bản, trở thành tượng đài. Lực trung tâm của Kurita là đòn kết liễu. Năm thiết giáp hạm, 10 tàu tuần dương hạng nặng, hai tàu tuần dương hạng nhẹ, 15 tàu khu trục đóng gần Singapore vì Các tàu ngầm của Mỹ đã làm giảm lượng nhiên liệu dự trữ của các hòn đảo quê hương Nhật Bản xuống mức nhỏ giọt. Và hạm đội phải ở gần nguồn cung cấp của nó. Đây không phải là một hạm đội được cử đi chiến đấu bình đẳng. Đây là lần ném xúc xắc cuối cùng của Đế chế và nó đang tiến thẳng vào lối đi Palawan. Hai tàu ngầm Mỹ đang chờ đợi. Mặc dù vào giờ này cả phi hành đoàn vẫn chưa biết chính xác họ đang chờ đợi điều gì. USS Darter là tàu ngầm lớp Gateau dài 311 ft được đóng ở Groutton, Connecticut. Được đưa vào hoạt động vào tháng 9 năm 1943. Nó mang theo 24 quả ngư lôi trong 10 ống, sáu quả phía trước, bốn quả phía ngoài và một cơ khí não gọi là máy tính dữ liệu mục tiêu xử lý tốc độ, phạm vi và tốc độ thành giải pháp bắn. Thuyền trưởng của cô là Chỉ huy David Haywood Mcclintok, 32 tuổi. Ông đã trải qua những năm đầu tiên và nguy hiểm nhất của cuộc chiến tranh tàu ngầm Thái Bình Dương để tấn công quân Nhật tàu chiến mang ngư lôi thường xuyên không chịu nổ và các đô đốc không chịu nghe khiếu nại về họ. Anh ta đã giành được một ngôi sao bạc khi tấn công một tàu tuần dương Nhật Bản ở cự ly gần trong giao tranh bề mặt ban đêm. Phi hành đoàn của anh ấy xét về mọi mặt đều yêu mến anh ấy. Anh ta có trí thông minh khô khan và thần kinh ổn định và họ đã học được sự khác biệt giữa hai người. USS Dace là đối tác của anh ấy. Cùng lớp, cùng loại vũ khí do Chỉ huy Bladen Claget chỉ huy. Và hai chiếc thuyền cùng nhau tạo thành một bầy Sói với Mcccleinto nắm quyền kiểm soát chiến thuật. Họ đang tuần tra Palawan Passage, một kênh nước sâu rộng 35 đến 40 dặm chạy giữa đảo Paloan về phía đông và Biển Đông về phía tây. Rìa phía tây của kênh đó được đánh dấu trên mọi hải đồ đáng tin cậy bằng một cụm từ xuất hiện nhiều lần và không bao giờ được coi là thơ. Các biểu đồ gọi đó là vùng đất nguy hiểm.
